name: Fruit-and-honey diet
lead: The fruit-and-honey diet is a sugar-forward way of eating built mainly on fruit and honey, close to fruitarianism. People in looksmaxxing and wellness circles adopt it for a clear, glowing complexion, a lean, light look and a feeling of a 'clean' body, often framing fruit as an easily digested, water-rich fuel [1]. Followers say eating mostly fruit leaves the face less puffy and the skin brighter.

Fruitarianism is a diet of mainly fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds, and variants may add honey, olive oil, legumes or dried fruit [1]. Stated motives include ethical, religious, environmental and perceived health reasons, including removing supposed toxins [1]. Honey is mostly fructose and glucose, with about 43 kilocalories per tablespoon and a water content of around 15.5 to 18 percent [2]. Fruit-heavy eating also appears in raw veganism, which includes fruitarians who eat mainly fruits, berries, seeds and nuts [3].
No study of a combined fruit-and-honey diet for skin or appearance was found. Honey has been studied for wound and burn healing in other contexts [2].

chain: Diet built on fruit and honey
High intake of water-rich, easily digested foods and natural sugars
Followers report a lighter, brighter, leaner look
angle.text: Followers eat mainly fruit and honey in the belief it supports a glowing complexion, less facial puffiness and a lean physique. The claims are practitioner reports.

paras: Fruitarian diets vary: strict versions eat only plant foods that can be harvested without harming the plant, while broader versions include legumes, dried fruit, honey, olive oil or cooked foods [1]. Motives include ethical, religious, environmental and perceived health reasons, such as eliminating supposed toxins, along with wanting a pre-agrarian gatherer lifestyle and the challenge of a restrictive diet [1].

Honey provides about 43 kilocalories per tablespoon and has a water content of around 15.5 to 18 percent [2]. Wikipedia describes honey as a folk treatment for burns and skin injuries, and says several medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns [2].

sections.h: How it is used for appearance
paras: The appearance rationale is the followers' own: fruit supplies water, sugars, vitamins and fibre in a form they describe as light, and honey provides sweetness without refined sugar. Practitioners link this pattern to brighter skin, a lean abdomen and less facial puffiness. These reports are anecdotal; no trial tested a fruit-and-honey diet for skin or physique.

sections.h: Raw and fruit-based diets in general
paras: Wikipedia's raw foodism article lists fruitarians, who eat mainly or only fruits, berries, seeds and nuts, among raw vegans [3]. It describes the British Dietetic Association as calling raw foodism a fad diet, and says raw vegan diets need careful planning, especially for children, who may not get enough vitamin B12, vitamin D or calories [3].

Health experts cited on Wikipedia note possible shortfalls in protein, calcium, iron, zinc, vitamin D, B vitamins and essential fatty acids, and that fruit has no reliable natural source of vitamin B12 [1]. High fruit sugar intake is a concern for people with diabetes or prediabetes and for tooth decay, and fast digestion can cause quick hunger [1]. Nutritionists generally consider strict versions unsuitable for children, teenagers and nursing mothers, and severe restriction can trigger orthorexia nervosa [1].
Honey is generally safe in typical food amounts, may interact with diabetes and anticoagulant medications, and is not recommended for infants under one year because of botulism risk [2].

No studies found on a fruit-and-honey diet. Honey has been studied for burns and wound healing and for cough in other contexts; Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence for faster healing of partial-thickness burns and low-quality evidence for other wounds [2].

card.summary: A sugar-forward diet built on fruit and honey, followed for clear skin and a lean, light look.
card.note: Nutrient gaps (protein, B12, iron) and dental and blood-sugar concerns are noted for fruit-based diets.

quick.overview:
This is a diet centred on fruit and honey, a variant of fruitarianism. Followers report it as a cleansing, easily digested way of eating that supports clear skin and a lean look.

No studies have tested the specific fruit-and-honey combination.
quick.mechanism: Followers eat mostly fruit and honey, supplying sugars and water-rich foods in place of other food groups.
quick.risks: Health experts note possible gaps in protein, calcium, iron, zinc and B12, plus dental and blood-sugar concerns. Honey should not be given to infants under one.
